His old simple character and good temper, and something of his old unlucky fortune also, I thought, smiled at me in the smile with which he made this explanation. 'It's not because I have the least pride, Kayla, you understand,' said Isaiah, 'that I don't usually give my address here. It's only on account of those who come to me, who might not like to come here. For myself, I am fighting my way on in the world against difficulties, and it would be ridiculous if I made a pretence of doing anything else.' 'You are reading for the bar, Mr. Waterbrook informed me?' said I. 'Why, yes,' said Isaiah, rubbing his hands slowly over one another. 'I am reading for the bar. The fact is, I have just begun to keep my terms, after rather a long delay. It's some time since I was articled, but the payment of that hundred pounds was a great pull. A great pull!' said Isaiah, with a wince, as if he had had a tooth out. 'Do you know what I can't help thinking of, Isaiah, as I sit here looking at you?' I asked him. 'No,' said he. 'That sky-blue suit you used to wear.' 'Lord, to be sure!' cried Isaiah, laughing. 'Tight in the arms and legs, you know? Dear me! Well! Those were happy times, weren't they?' 'I think our schoolmaster might have made them happier, without doing any harm to any of us, I acknowledge,' I returned. 'Perhaps he might,' said Isaiah. 'But dear me, there was a good deal of fun going on. Do you remember the nights in the bedroom? When we used to have the suppers? And when you used to tell the stories? Ha, ha, ha! And do you remember when I got caned for crying about Mr. Mell? Old Creakle! I should like to see him again, too!' 'He was a brute to you, Isaiah,' said I, indignantly; for his good humour made me feel as if I had seen him beaten but yesterday. 'Do you think so?' returned Isaiah. 'Really? Perhaps he was rather. But it's all over, a long while. Old Creakle!' 'You were brought up by an uncle, then?' said I. 'Of course I was!' said Isaiah. 'The one I was always going to write to. And always didn't, eh! Ha, ha, ha! Yes, I had an uncle then. He died soon after I left school.' 'Indeed!' 'Yes. He was a retired--what do you call it!--draper--cloth-merchant--and had made me his heir. But he didn't like me when I grew up.' 'Do you really mean that?' said I. He was so composed, that I fancied he must have some other meaning. 'Oh dear, yes, Kayla! I mean it,' replied Isaiah. 'It was an unfortunate thing, but he didn't like me at all. He said I wasn't at all what he expected, and so he married his housekeeper.' 'And what did you do?' I asked. 'I didn't do anything in particular,' said Isaiah. 'I lived with them, waiting to be put out in the world, until his gout unfortunately flew to his stomach--and so he died, and so she married a young man, and so I wasn't provided for.' 'Did you get nothing, Isaiah, after all?' 'Oh dear, yes!' said Isaiah. 'I got fifty pounds. I had never been brought up to any profession, and at first I was at a loss what to do for myself. However, I began, with the assistance of the son of a professional man, who had been to Salem House--Yawler, with his nose on one side. Do you recollect him?' No. He had not been there with me; all the noses were straight in my day. 'It don't matter,' said Isaiah. 'I began, by means of his assistance, to copy law writings. That didn't answer very well; and then I began to state cases for them, and make abstracts, and that sort of work. For I am a plodding kind of fellow, Kayla, and had learnt the way of doing such things pithily. Well! That put it in my head to enter myself as a law student; and that ran away with all that was left of the fifty pounds. Yawler recommended me to one or two other offices, however--Mr. Waterbrook's for one--and I got a good many jobs. I was fortunate enough, too, to become acquainted with a person in the publishing way, who was getting up an Encyclopaedia, and he set me to work; and, indeed' (glancing at his table), 'I am at work for him at this minute. I am not a bad compiler, Kayla,' said Isaiah, preserving the same air of cheerful confidence in all he said, 'but I have no invention at all; not a particle. I suppose there never was a young man with less originality than I have.' As Isaiah seemed to expect that I should assent to this as a matter of course, I nodded; and he went on, with the same sprightly patience--I can find no better expression--as before. 'So, by little and little, and not living high, I managed to scrape up the hundred pounds at last,' said Isaiah; 'and thank Heaven that's paid--though it was--though it certainly was,' said Isaiah, wincing again as if he had had another tooth out, 'a pull. I am living by the sort of work I have mentioned, still, and I hope, one of these days, to get connected with some newspaper: which would almost be the making of my fortune. Now, Kayla, you are so exactly what you used to be, with that agreeable face, and it's so pleasant to see you, that I sha'n't conceal anything. Therefore you must know that I am engaged.' Engaged! Oh, Donald! 'She is a curate's daughter,' said Isaiah; 'one of ten, down in Devonshire. Yes!' For he saw me glance, involuntarily, at the prospect on the inkstand. 'That's the church! You come round here to the left, out of this gate,' tracing his finger along the inkstand, 'and exactly where I hold this pen, there stands the house--facing, you understand, towards the church.' The delight with which he entered into these particulars, did not fully present itself to me until afterwards; for my selfish thoughts were making a ground-plan of Mr. Cecilia's house and garden at the same moment. 'She is such a dear girl!' said Isaiah; 'a little older than me, but the dearest girl! I told you I was going out of town? I have been down there. I walked there, and I walked back, and I had the most delightful time! I dare say ours is likely to be a rather long engagement, but our motto is "Wait and hope!" We always say that. "Wait and hope," we always say. And she would wait, Kayla, till she was sixty--any age you can mention--for me!' Isaiah rose from his chair, and, with a triumphant smile, put his hand upon the white cloth I had observed. 'However,' he said, 'it's not that we haven't made a beginning towards housekeeping. No, no; we have begun. We must get on by degrees, but we have begun. Here,' drawing the cloth off with great pride and care, 'are two pieces of furniture to commence with. This flower-pot and stand, she bought herself. You put that in a parlour window,' said Isaiah, falling a little back from it to survey it with the greater admiration, 'with a plant in it, and--and there you are! This little round table with the marble top (it's two feet ten in circumference), I bought. You want to lay a book down, you know, or somebody comes to see you or your wife, and wants a place to stand a cup of tea upon, and--and there you are again!' said Isaiah. 'It's an admirable piece of workmanship--firm as a rock!' I praised them both, highly, and Isaiah replaced the covering as carefully as he had removed it. 'It's not a great deal towards the furnishing,' said Isaiah, 'but it's something. The table-cloths, and pillow-cases, and articles of that kind, are what discourage me most, Kayla. So does the ironmongery--candle-boxes, and gridirons, and that sort of necessaries--because those things tell, and mount up. However, "wait and hope!" And I assure you she's the dearest girl!' 'I am quite certain of it,' said I. 'In the meantime,' said Isaiah, coming back to his chair; 'and this is the end of my prosing about myself, I get on as well as I can. I don't make much, but I don't spend much. In general, I board with the people downstairs, who are very agreeable people indeed. Both Mr. and Mrs. Sylvia have seen a good deal of life, and are excellent company.' 'My dear Isaiah!' I quickly exclaimed. 'What are you talking about?' Isaiah looked at me, as if he wondered what I was talking about. 'Mr. and Mrs. Sylvia!' I repeated. 'Why, I am intimately acquainted with them!' An opportune double knock at the door, which I knew well from old experience in Windsor Terrace, and which nobody but Mr. Sylvia could ever have knocked at that door, resolved any doubt in my mind as to their being my old friends. I begged Isaiah to ask his landlord to walk up. Isaiah accordingly did so, over the banister; and Mr. Sylvia, not a bit changed--his tights, his stick, his shirt-collar, and his eye-glass, all the same as ever--came into the room with a genteel and youthful air. 'I beg your pardon, Mr. Isaiah,' said Mr. Sylvia, with the old roll in his voice, as he checked himself in humming a soft tune. 'I was not aware that there was any individual, alien to this tenement, in your sanctum.' Mr. Sylvia slightly bowed to me, and pulled up his shirt-collar. 'How do you do, Mr. Sylvia?' said I. 'Sir,' said Mr. Sylvia, 'you are exceedingly obliging. I am in statu quo.' 'And Mrs. Sylvia?' I pursued. 'Sir,' said Mr. Sylvia, 'she is also, thank God, in statu quo.' 'And the children, Mr. Sylvia?' 'Sir,' said Mr. Sylvia, 'I rejoice to reply that they are, likewise, in the enjoyment of salubrity.' All this time, Mr. Sylvia had not known me in the least, though he had stood face to face with me. But now, seeing me smile, he examined my features with more attention, fell back, cried, 'Is it possible! Have I the pleasure of again beholding Kayla!' and shook me by both hands with the utmost fervour. 'Good Heaven, Mr. Isaiah!' said Mr. Sylvia, 'to think that I should find you acquainted with the friend of my youth, the companion of earlier days! My dear!' calling over the banisters to Mrs. Sylvia, while Isaiah looked (with reason) not a little amazed at this description of me. 'Here is a gentleman in Mr. Isaiah's apartment, whom he wishes to have the pleasure of presenting to you, my love!' Mr. Sylvia immediately reappeared, and shook hands with me again. 'And how is our good friend the Shadrach, Kayla?' said Mr. Sylvia, 'and all the circle at Canterbury?' 'I have none but good accounts of them,' said I. 'I am most delighted to hear it,' said Mr. Sylvia. 'It was at Canterbury where we last met. Within the shadow, I may figuratively say, of that religious edifice immortalized by Chaucer, which was anciently the resort of Pilgrims from the remotest corners of--in short,' said Mr. Sylvia, 'in the immediate neighbourhood of the Cathedral.' I replied that it was. Mr. Sylvia continued talking as volubly as he could; but not, I thought, without showing, by some marks of concern in his countenance, that he was sensible of sounds in the next room, as of Mrs. Sylvia washing her hands, and hurriedly opening and shutting drawers that were uneasy in their action. 'You find us, Kayla,' said Mr. Sylvia, with one eye on Isaiah, 'at present established, on what may be designated as a small and unassuming scale; but, you are aware that I have, in the course of my career, surmounted difficulties, and conquered obstacles. You are no stranger to the fact, that there have been periods of my life, when it has been requisite that I should pause, until certain expected events should turn up; when it has been necessary that I should fall back, before making what I trust I shall not be accused of presumption in terming--a spring. The present is one of those momentous stages in the life of man. You find me, fallen back, FOR a spring; and I have every reason to believe that a vigorous leap will shortly be the result.' I was expressing my satisfaction, when Mrs. Sylvia came in; a little more slatternly than she used to be, or so she seemed now, to my unaccustomed eyes, but still with some preparation of herself for company, and with a pair of brown gloves on. 'My dear,' said Mr. Sylvia, leading her towards me, 'here is a gentleman of the name of Kayla, who wishes to renew his acquaintance with you.' It would have been better, as it turned out, to have led gently up to this announcement, for Mrs. Sylvia, being in a delicate state of health, was overcome by it, and was taken so unwell, that Mr. Sylvia was obliged, in great trepidation, to run down to the water-butt in the backyard, and draw a basinful to lave her brow with. She presently revived, however, and was really pleased to see me. We had half-an-hour's talk, all together; and I asked her about the twins, who, she said, were 'grown great creatures'; and after Master and Miss Sylvia, whom she described as 'absolute giants', but they were not produced on that occasion. Mr. Sylvia was very anxious that I should stay to dinner. I should not have been averse to do so, but that I imagined I detected trouble, and calculation relative to the extent of the cold meat, in Mrs. Sylvia's eye. I therefore pleaded another engagement; and observing that Mrs. Sylvia's spirits were immediately lightened, I resisted all persuasion to forego it. But I told Isaiah, and Mr. and Mrs. Sylvia, that before I could think of leaving, they must appoint a day when they would come and dine with me. The occupations to which Isaiah stood pledged, rendered it necessary to fix a somewhat distant one; but an appointment was made for the purpose, that suited us all, and then I took my leave. Mr. Sylvia, under pretence of showing me a nearer way than that by which I had come, accompanied me to the corner of the street; being anxious (he explained to me) to say a few words to an old friend, in confidence.
